newsitem.title: UK: UK budget expected to deliver only modest tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK budget expected to deliver only modest tax cuts.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will announce his annual budget in two days' time and a consensus is hardening that he will unveil only modest tax cuts, a tactic his predecessor backs wholeheartedly.
Clarke will end weeks of speculation among British politicians, financial markets and the man on the street when he stands up to deliver his budget on Tuesday.

Financial pundits and the national press believe he will deliver an eye-catching one penny cut in the basic rate of income tax, but that aside will only tinker with the tax system, allowing room to increase spending on the politically sensitive health and education sectors.
No-one is expecting tax cuts to be entirely absent from the budget with elections due within six months and Clarke's ruling Conservative Party trailing badly in the polls.
But with high street spending rocketing, many experts fear a giveaway budget would overheat the economy.
Norman Lamont, Clarke's predecessor as finance minister, added his voice to the chorus calling for a prudent budget.
"I don't think the public finances are in such a strong position that we can have significant tax cuts that aren't matched by cuts in spending," he said on Sky TV.
"I don't think there will be significant spending cuts, so I hope the Chancellor will not go in for significant tax cuts."
Despite a massive 4.4 billion pounds repayment of government debt last month, Britain's public sector deficit has stubbornly refused to shrink as expected.

In July, Clarke was forced to increase his forecast deficit for this year to 27 billion pounds ($45.48 billion) from an initial 22.5 billion. He may well revise that forecast back down on Tuesday but it is clear the room for tax cuts is cramped.

London-based economists certainly expect few pre-election fireworks from the budget. A Reuter poll of 27 economists found a consensus expecting tax cuts to the tune of 2.25 billion pounds, matched by planned cuts in government spending.
That would allow Clarke to cut the basic rate of income tax by one penny to 23 percent, but not much else.
He is expected to increase the personal allowance on individual incomes which is tax free, however. For now, the first 3,765 pounds of personal incomes are untaxed.
And he is also tipped to widen the income band on which the 20 percent starting rate of income tax is levied.

Gordon Brown, the opposition Labour Party's finance spokesman, said he would lower the starting rate of tax. "The first tax cut that should be made, if there is scope, should be on VAT on fuel," he told Sky Television. "My second idea, for the longer-term, would be a lower starting rate of income tax."
Value-added-tax on fuel bills is levied at eight percent.
Whatever Clarke comes up with, the British weekend press was abuzz with speculation.

The Guardian newspaper stuck rigidly to the consensus, forecasting a two billion pound package of spending cuts to allow a one penny income tax reduction. Clarke would launch a crackdown on fraudulent claims for welfare payments, it said.
The Sunday Times and Sunday Telegraph also expected a one penny income tax cut. The Financial Times agreed but said there was some possibility of a two pence reduction.

Only The Independent newspaper stood out from the crowd. It said Clarke could slash income tax by three pence in the pound. But the Sunday Times quoted Treasury sources as saying that suggestion was "very, very mad."
The Sunday Telegraph said modest tax cuts and higher personal allowances would be paid for by higher fuel and tobacco duties and possible curbs on profit-related pay schemes.

PRP links a portion of salaries to a company's performance and attracts tax relief. Although unlikely to be abolished altogether, experts have estimated the government could save about 1.5 billion pounds by doing so.
On the spending side of the equation, the politically sacred cows of health and education were safe from the axe, most of the newspapers said.

Lamont said the government would fight the next election on the basis of economic competence not tax handouts. "I think the public will respond if the Chancellor says he is going to be responsible. The important thing is to keep the recovery going."
To that end, the Sunday Times forecast Clarke would raise next year's economic growth forecast to 3.5 percent, from 3.25.

And just in case he feels the temptations to shower the British electorate with tax reductions, the Sunday Telegraph pointed out that such a move would almost certainly trigger further interest rate rises -- political poison in a country where about two thirds of homes are owned, not rented. ($1=.5937 Pound)
